title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the stop that changes everything

questions.prompt: In which of these sentences can the -ing form be replaced by to + infinitive with NO change of meaning?

options.text: She continued talking about the launch.
We can't stand waiting at the gate.

questions.explanation: Continue, prefer and can't stand belong to the small group of verbs that accept both forms and mean the same thing either way: she continued to talk, they prefer to travel, we can't stand to wait. Stop is the exception the whole lesson is built on: "he stopped to watch the countdown" would say that he broke off something else in order to watch it, and "the crew stopped to take photographs" that they interrupted their work for the camera. Neither is what the -ing form says. With stop, changing the form changes the story.

questions.prompt: A log book reads: "10:12 — Amine stopped reading the checklist. 10:14 — Sonia stopped to read the checklist." At 10:15, who has the checklist open?
questions.explanation: The two forms send the sentence in opposite directions. "Stopped reading" cancels the activity named by the -ing form, so at 10:12 Amine closed the checklist and is not reading afterwards. "Stopped to read" gives the purpose of the interruption, so at 10:14 Sonia broke off whatever else she was doing in order to open it. One minute later only Sonia is reading, and the whole difference lies in the little word to, which after stop means "in order to".

questions.prompt: Put the five parts in order to make one correct sentence.
questions.explanation: The sentence reads: The company has postponed sending its first tourists into orbit until next spring. Postpone is followed directly by a verb in the -ing form, so "sending" must sit against it — "postponed to send" and "postponed its first tourists sending" are both impossible. Once the -ing form is in place the sentence continues like any other: the people it acts on, then where they were going, then the new date.

questions.prompt: A spaceport's website says: "Every passenger must finish paying the full fare sixty days before the flight. Passengers who risk missing the medical check on the morning of departure lose their seat. We do not mind postponing your booking once, but a second change involves paying a new fee." A passenger changes his booking for the second time. What does the notice say he must do?

options.text: Lose his seat on the flight.
Pay the whole fare sixty days earlier.

questions.explanation: "A second change involves paying a new fee": involve is one of the verbs followed by a verb in the -ing form, and here it announces what the second change brings with it — money, and nothing else. The seat is lost only by a passenger who risks missing the medical check on the morning of departure, and the sixty-day rule concerns the fare itself, not a change of booking. Read the -ing form that follows each verb: it names exactly the action the sentence is about.

questions.prompt: English does not choose between un- and in- by any rule: each word keeps the prefix it has always had. Which line gives BOTH opposites correctly?
questions.explanation: Clear takes un- and convenient takes in-, and nothing in their spelling or their sound predicts it: unclear and inconvenient simply have to be learnt as words. The rule that does exist covers only il-, im- and ir-, which are chosen by the first letter of the word, as in illegal, impatient and irregular. Everywhere else the dictionary decides and the ear misleads — compare unpleasant with inexpensive, or unfit with ineffective.

questions.prompt: Say this proverb in your own words: "The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only a page." Which restatement keeps its meaning?

options.text: Reading books is a good way of discovering foreign countries.
Travellers have no time left for reading and study.
Someone who never travels sees only a tiny part of the world.
You should read at least one page of a book on every journey.

questions.explanation: Paraphrasing a proverb means dropping the image and keeping the idea. Here the image compares the world to a book and one country to a single page of it, so the idea is that a person who stays at home discovers almost nothing of what exists. The restatements about reading books, about studying or about a page a day have kept the words of the image and lost what it stands for — and that is the trap every proverb sets.
